subject: Discovery recap — tool calling & structured output (JSON schema)
messages:
From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Reed <samantha.reed@brightcorp.com>, Michael Chen <mchen@brightcorp.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>, Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 10:12:00 -0500
Subject: Discovery recap — tool calling & structured output (JSON schema)

Hi Samantha / Michael — thanks again for taking time today. Quick recap from our discovery call and proposed next steps so we’re all aligned.

What we heard (pain points):
- You need deterministic, schema-conformant responses for downstream automation (order intake + fulfillment).
- Current LLM outputs include free-form text that requires expensive parsing and manual QA.
- You have multi-step agent workflows that must call internal tools (inventory, pricing, approvals) and return structured JSON payloads to the orchestration layer.

Current stack:
- Backend: Ruby on Rails + Postgres; async worker queue (Sidekiq).
- Integrations: internal inventory API, ERP via middleware, Slack for human approvals.
- Hosting: GCP us-central1.

Success criteria (how BrightCorp will measure a win):
1) Generated outputs validate 100% against a provided JSON schema (no schema violations) for 90%+ of calls during PoC.
2) Latency: median end-to-end response <= 800ms for single-step tool calls under PoC load (50 RPS burst).
3) Deterministic formatting: fixed field ordering and no unexpected top-level keys for downstream consumer.
4) Observable and auditable tool calls (timestamps, tool name, args) for each agent action.

Technical notes discussed:
- Function/tool calling model: Redwood can expose a tool-calling interface where models return explicit tool_call objects (name + args). We’ll map those to your inventory/pricing endpoints.
- Structured output enforcement: use strict JSON schema validation at the runtime boundary and post-process to drop/flag non-conforming responses. We discussed a strategy to have the model output a top-level wrapper: {"result": <payload>, "meta": {"tool_calls": [...]} } to keep runtime consistency.
- Edge cases: ambiguous user prompts will trigger a deterministic clarification flow (explicit follow-up question) rather than free-form guessing.

Attachments: I’ve attached a short discovery template and an example agent workflow JSON to capture the schema and sequence we discussed.

Next steps (agreed):
- Demo access + PoC environment: Redwood to provision sandbox keys and a small Dedicated instance for BrightCorp (SLA-lite) — action: Jordan to send invite and PoC checklist (today).
- Schema: BrightCorp to share canonical JSON schema(s) for order payload + agent tool interface by EOD Thursday — action: Samantha.
- Technical deep-dive: schedule a 60-min call with engineering to map tool endpoints and auth flow (next week) — action: Laura to coordinate.
- Quick bench: Redwood to run a short runbook validating model outputs against the provided schema once received — action: Soojin.

If I missed anything or you want changes to the success criteria, please flag. Happy to jump on a quick call.

Thanks —
Jordan Blake
Enterprise Sales (West) | Redwood Inference
jordan.blake@redwood.com | (415) 555-0112

From: Samantha Reed <samantha.reed@brightcorp.com>
To: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Michael Chen <mchen@brightcorp.com>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Tue, 10 Feb 2026 14:03:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Discovery recap — tool calling & structured output (JSON schema)

Jordan — thanks for the clear recap, this aligns with what we discussed. A few clarifications and notes from our side: 

1) Schema: we have two schemas — OrderCreate and ApprovalRequest. I’ll share canonical JSON Schema files and example valid payloads by Thursday. The top-level wrapper you suggested looks good; we prefer the property order to be stable for our ingestion layer.
2) Edge cases: when an agent cannot determine a SKU, we want it to call the inventory_tool with {"query":"..."} rather than inventing values. That call should appear in the meta.tool_calls array.
3) Security: all API calls must use our service account with short-lived signed tokens. We’ll share the details in the tech doc.

We are open to starting PoC with a small volume (10 RPS) and ramping. The 50 RPS target for performance is a longer-term goal.

One ask: can Redwood provide a small example of a deterministic output enforcement strategy (pseudo code or config) — that’d help our engineers evaluate integration effort quickly.

Best,
Samantha Reed
Head of Automation | BrightCorp
samantha.reed@brightcorp.com

From: Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Reed <samantha.reed@brightcorp.com>, Michael Chen <mchen@brightcorp.com>
Cc: Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>, Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Feb 2026 08:21:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Discovery recap — tool calling & structured output (JSON schema) — PoC artifacts attached

Thanks Samantha — appreciate the clarifications. Per your ask, attaching a short example agent workflow (example-agent-workflow.json) and a one-page pseudo-code snippet in the discovery template that shows deterministic enforcement. Summary of what we’ll provide for PoC: 
- Sandbox keys and a PoC checklist + runbook.
- A Redwood runtime preconfigured to validate outputs against your JSON Schema and reject/flag invalid responses. We’ll include logs showing validation failures and examples of fixed prompts used to coerce schema compliance.
- Tool-call audit: runtime will emit a structured audit entry for every inferred tool call (tool name, args, timestamp, request_id).

Action items updated: 
- Jordan: send invite and provision sandbox (in progress).
- Samantha: share canonical JSON Schema + service-account token exchange details (by Thu).
- Laura: propose 3 time slots for engineering deep-dive (today).
- Soojin & Aditya: once schema is in, run initial validation tests and report pass rate (target >= 90%).

Proposed blocking criteria for PoC stop: if 1) schema pass rate < 60% after three tuning iterations, or 2) median latency > 1500ms under PoC load. We’ll keep these thresholds configurable.

Thanks — we’ll follow up with calendar invites.

Jordan Blake
Enterprise Sales | Redwood Inference

From: Soojin Lee <soojin.lee@redwood.com>
To: Samantha Reed <samantha.reed@brightcorp.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan.blake@redwood.com>
Cc: Aditya Rao <aditya_rao@redwood.com>, Laura Bennett <laura.bennett@redwood.com>
Date: Wed, 11 Feb 2026 09:05:00 -0500
Subject: Re: Discovery recap — deterministic enforcement approach and next steps

Samantha / team — quick technical follow-up from my side. A few specifics we’ll need when you share the schema to ensure the PoC runs smoothly: 

1) Canonical schema files (JSON Schema draft-07 or later) and a few realistic example payloads (happy path + 5 edge cases).
2) Expected field ordering preference (we can enforce ordering at serialization if you give us the canonical order).
3) Tool endpoint definitions: path, method, auth type, sample request/response for inventory_tool and approve_tool.
4) Error handling policy: how should the agent behave on 4xx/5xx from tool calls (retry, escalate to human)?

Deterministic enforcement approach (high level):
- Step A: Model returns structured wrapper with result + meta.tool_calls.
- Step B: Runtime validates "result" against your JSON Schema. If valid -> serialize using canonical key order and forward.
- Step C: If invalid -> runtime generates a constrained clarification prompt (template attached) and retries N times (configurable) before raising to human operator.

I'll run a short smoke test once we have the schema. Can we aim to have the schema and example payloads by Thu EOD so we can schedule the engineering deep-dive for next Tue/Wed?

Thanks,
Soojin Lee
Solutions Engineer | Redwood Inference
soojin.lee@redwood.com
